content: The cost associated with transient infections that resolve quickly is notable. Following an initial peak, the prevalence of infections gradually declines to a stable level among middle-aged women. In certain populations, a less pronounced second peak in older women has been observed. In two large studies conducted in Central America, this second peak was found to be comparable in magnitude to the first peak. A study by Denny in 2008, conducted in South Africa, reviewed the burden of cervical cancer in the region. It highlighted that cervical cancer remains the most common cancer among South African women, particularly those with limited access to cervical cancer screening. However, the sources searched, inclusion criteria, and total studies included were not reported. Li's 2019 study, a systematic review conducted in China, examined the epidemiology of high-risk HPV among mainland Chinese women. The study included healthy women undergoing routine cervical lesion screening, women visiting hospitals for suspicious cervical lesions, and women diagnosed with cervical cancer or precancerous cervical lesions. HPV DNA was detected using PCR. Observational studies published in English or Chinese between January 2010 and June 2018 were included. Tainio's 2018 systematic review and meta-analysis, conducted in the UK, estimated the regression, persistence, and progression of untreated cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 (CIN2) lesions. The study included data from Medline, Embase, and CINAHL from January 1973 to August 2016. It focused on non-pregnant women with histologically confirmed CIN2 lesions managed conservatively for at least three months. Regression rates were higher, and progression rates were lower in women under 30 years of age compared to older women. For women under 30, regression at 24 months was 60%, increasing to 70% at 36 months, with a progression rate of 11% at 24 months. In women over 30, regression at 24 months was 44%, with a progression rate of 23%. Zhu's 2019 systematic review in China explored temporal trends and geographical patterns in HPV infection epidemiology, as well as differences between China and other countries. The study included data from PubMed, Web of Science, Chinese Scientific Journals Full Text Database, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and Wanfang Data. Inclusion criteria required studies to focus on the general population, include both high-risk and low-risk HPV types, explicitly state HPV detection methodologies, and report HPV prevalence or provide data to calculate estimates. A total of 68 studies were included, with 12 databases reporting age-specific prevalence of high-risk HPV infection. In a pooled analysis by Basu in 2013, the prevalence of CIN3 remained constant after the age of 40, while the prevalence of invasive cervical cancer increased gradually with age, peaking in the 60–65 age group. Adenocarcinoma was detected in only four cases, two of which occurred in women aged 35–40 and two in women aged 40–45. Several studies have examined barriers to cervical cancer screening. For example, in a US study by Sirovich in 2005, 65% of women who had undergone cervical screening believed they would never stop having Pap smears. Younger women were more likely to think they would continue screening indefinitely compared to older women. Perceptions of risk and personal experiences with cervical cancer influenced women's intentions to continue screening. In a Swedish study by Ostensson in 2015, younger women (29 years or younger) were more knowledgeable about HPV than older women. Similarly, in a Chinese study by Yanyue in 2018, older women (>40 years) had higher levels of knowledge about cervical cancer, while younger women (≤29 years) had greater awareness of HPV. Barriers to screening include embarrassment, fear of discomfort, and logistical challenges. Older women were less concerned about logistical issues than younger women. In a systematic review by Hope in 2017, knowledge levels, perceived barriers, and perceptions of cancer influenced older women's decisions to attend cervical screening. Misconceptions about the purpose of screening and low awareness of its benefits were observed across age groups. In Italy, a study by Bucchi in 2019 found that cervical cancer was diagnosed at a younger age in foreign-born women compared to Italian-born women. The median age at diagnosis was 59 years for Italian-born women and 47 years for foreign-born women. These findings underscore the importance of targeted public health initiatives to address barriers, improve knowledge, and enhance compliance with cervical cancer screening guidelines across different age groups and populations.
